headline: High: shared API/MCP-style integration can create prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-action risks; no direct sandbox evidence reduces confidence.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Kotaemon ingests documents/HTML/MHTML and serves a web UI over files in ./ktem_app_data, while MemMachine exposes an MCP Server and REST/Python SDK. That creates a plausible bridge where content from one can be treated as instructions by the other, especially if outputs are copied into shared workflows. No direct provenance controls are documented, so uncertainty pushes this above low.
conditions: IF MemMachine ingests Kotaemon-produced text through MCP or REST without provenance tagging, prompt injection is possible.
IF both agents are connected through a shared workspace or copy-paste workflow, attacker-controlled content can cross the boundary.
mitigations: Disable automatic ingestion of agent outputs into downstream prompts.
Add provenance labels to all retrieved documents and agent outputs.
Restrict MCP methods to read-only where possible.
Review and sanitize HTML/MHTML before passing to MemMachine.
requires-engineering: add content-trust checks between the two agents.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Kotaemon touches API keys and broad document types, and MemMachine stores long-term user facts and conversational context. If they share a workspace or if Kotaemon forwards file contents into third-party APIs while MemMachine retains context, sensitive material can flow across both systems. The profiles do not show isolation or DLP, so a default-safe assumption is not justified.
conditions: IF Kotaemon indexes documents containing secrets and MemMachine receives those outputs, leakage can occur.
IF MemMachine persists conversational context that includes Kotaemon-derived sensitive text, retention expands exposure.
mitigations: Separate the agents into distinct workspaces.
Block secrets from being indexed or summarized.
Turn off or narrow any shared logging of prompts and outputs.
Use redaction before passing documents between agents.
requires-engineering: enforce DLP on inter-agent transfers.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Kotaemon has broad network egress and file access to ./ktem_app_data, while MemMachine has allowlisted egress and MCP/API access. The profiles do not show overlapping write access to the same directory or shared mutable resource, so a direct conflict is not established. Uncertainty remains because shared orchestration is undocumented, but the blast radius appears limited.
conditions: IF both agents are configured to write to the same directory or database, write conflicts can occur.
IF an orchestrator grants both agents the same mutable OAuth or filesystem scope, contention becomes possible.
mitigations: Assign separate storage paths to each agent.
Avoid shared mutable databases or git worktrees.
Run one agent at a time for write-heavy tasks.
Use file locks if a shared directory is unavoidable.
requires-engineering: add orchestration-level locking.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Kotaemon is a RAG/chatbot system that can generate cited answers from documents, and MemMachine is an agentic memory layer exposed through API/MCP interfaces. If MemMachine treats Kotaemon output as authoritative, errors can cascade into downstream actions or persistent memory. No verification step is documented, so the interaction is plausible in default integrations.
conditions: IF MemMachine stores or acts on Kotaemon-generated answers without verification, errors can persist and amplify.
IF downstream workflows use those answers for travel decisions or user-facing actions, the blast radius increases.
mitigations: Require human review before persisting agent-generated facts.
Add a verification step against source documents.
Mark Kotaemon outputs as untrusted until checked.
Limit MemMachine memory writes to confirmed facts only.
requires-engineering: implement confidence-gated downstream actions.

E_compliance.rationale: Kotaemon handles API keys and diverse document classes, while MemMachine stores long-term user facts and conversational context. The profiles do not show a residency, certification, or retention mismatch, so a concrete compliance breach is not proven. However, the combination suggests compliance-sensitive data may be processed by both, warranting caution rather than none.
conditions: IF regulated data such as PHI or EU PII is routed through both agents, compliance review is required.
IF retention settings differ between the two systems, subject-rights handling may diverge.
mitigations: Document the data classes each agent may process.
Align retention and deletion settings.
Exclude regulated data from shared workflows.
Review vendor DPAs and residency claims.
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for regulated data.
